author: reek
body: FAT over the payload's own block drivers (B3.2, FAT32 in H3b). The foreword `Fat16` chapter already knows FAT: its BPB parse, directory-entry decode, name matching, and path splitting are pure functions over a sector buffer, and this chapter reuses every one of them. What it cannot reuse is `Fat16`'s sector source: those functions call the `block-read-sector` builtin, which is a syscall. The Option A stub jumps straight to `opening` and configures no syscall path, so on this boot every read must go through `disk-read-sector` (AHCI, then legacy IDE).

author: reek
body: Reading a file writes bytes into a flat caller-supplied buffer. `Fat16`'s own reader accumulates a `List Integer` one byte at a time -- fine for a small config file, ruinous for a 2 MB seed, which is what B3.3 will ask for.

author: reek
body: The EFI System Partition's first LBA, found by walking the GPT: the header at LBA 1 names the partition-entry array, and the first entry whose type GUID is the ESP's carries the starting LBA. Returns 0 when the disk has no GPT or no ESP -- an honest zero, not a guess.

author: reek
body: Only the low 32 bits of each 64-bit GPT field are read: a boot medium with more than 2 TB of sectors before its ESP is not a stick.

author: reek
body: Four bytes of the type GUID are enough to name the ESP among the partition types a boot stick carries.

author: reek
body: A zero 16-bit FAT size is the structural mark of the 32-bit layout; the parse then maps FAT32's fields into the shared record as the chapter prose describes.

author: reek
body: The FAT32 root directory is an ordinary cluster chain named by the BPB, so its search IS the data-area search; only FAT16 has the fixed root region.

author: reek
body: A directory that lives in the data area is a cluster chain, so a miss in one cluster follows the FAT to the next.

author: reek
body: `e` is the entry matched at depth-1. A path continues only through a directory (attribute bit 4); a file in the middle of a path is a miss, not a silent success.

author: reek
body: Copy a file's bytes into `dest`, following the FAT chain. Returns the number of bytes written, which is the entry's size unless the chain ended early (a truncated or corrupt file -- report what was actually read, never what the directory claimed).

author: reek
body: Reading a 2 MB file one sector at a time costs two reads per sector: the data, and the FAT sector holding the next cluster. Instead load the FAT once, follow the chain in memory, and coalesce consecutive clusters into runs -- a freshly written file is contiguous, so a whole seed becomes a single bulk command (one DMA on AHCI). Fragmentation costs one command per run, never per sector.

author: reek
body: Length of the run of consecutive clusters starting at `cluster`, capped so a corrupt chain cannot spin: a run can never exceed the clusters the file still needs.

author: reek
body: Read a file into a caller-supplied buffer. The buffer must hold the file's size rounded up to a whole sector -- the last sector arrives whole, and trimming it is the caller's business.

author: reek
body: The 8.3 name is passed already space-padded to 11 characters, the way it sits in a directory entry ("IDENTITYDAT").

author: reek
body: The chain writer: the FAT is loaded once and the whole chain is built in memory, then flushed to both copies in bulk, then the data goes out in contiguous runs -- the write-side mirror of Bulk File Reading above. Every allocated cluster is marked end-of-chain the moment it is taken, so the free scan cannot hand the same cluster out twice, and the link to the next overwrites the mark as the chain grows; a volume that runs out mid-chain aborts before the flush, leaving the disk untouched.

author: reek
body: Writes are chunked at 64 sectors: a bulk transfer above 64 KB crosses the TRB boundary question rung 3 of the sitting ladder has never answered on metal, and a screenshot must not be the first thing to ask it.
